1331.title: Sita
1331.hook: the war is won, and Rama speaks harshly to Sita in front of everyone; she answers him, then asks for a fire
1331.howItsDone: Sita's ordeal by fire, the agni pariksha, is retold, staged and debated across Hindu traditions; Valmiki, Tulsidas and folk singers tell it in different ways, and Hindu teachers and readers continue to discuss what it means.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita in the ashoka grove: a blade of grass between her and Ravana, and a no to Hanuman's offer of a ride home.

The war is over. Ravana is dead. Sita is brought out in front of the whole army, and the reunion the story has been moving toward doesn't come. In Valmiki's sixth book, Rama speaks to her coldly, in public. He says, in paraphrase, that he fought to clear his name and his family's, and that she may go wherever she likes. It's a hard scene to read. Today isn't about defending it or explaining it away. It's about the woman who has to answer it, and what she says.
screen: `THE WAR IS OVER.` → `NO REUNION, A COLD SPEECH.` → `WHAT SITA SAYS BACK.`

segments.voice: Sita doesn't stay silent. She wipes her tears and speaks, and Valmiki gives her a full answer. In paraphrase: why do you speak to me like this, the way a common man speaks to a common woman? What was in my power, my heart, was always yours. What was not in my power, my body seized by force, was not my doing. If you meant to give me up, why didn't you say so when Hanuman came? I would have ended my life then, and spared you a war. Then she turns to Lakshmana and asks him to build a fire. She walks around Rama, faces the flames, calls on Agni, the god of fire, as her witness, and steps in. The fire god himself rises out of the flames carrying her, gives her back to Rama, and declares her faultless. Rama then says he never doubted her, and did this so the world would see. The tradition has not settled this scene. Some read the fire as Sita's victory: her truth proven before everyone. Some later retellings, including Tulsidas's Ramcharitmanas, tell it so that the real Sita was never in Lanka at all. Some readers, and some singers of these songs, simply sit with Sita's hurt and her courage. In the worst moment of her story, Valmiki gives Sita the clearest voice. She names what was hers and what wasn't. She asks her own question. Then she chooses the fire herself.
screen: `SHE WIPES HER TEARS AND SPEAKS` · `MY HEART WAS ALWAYS YOURS` · `SHE ASKS LAKSHMANA FOR A FIRE` · `THE TRADITION STILL ARGUING`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one hard thing that's been laid at your door, fairly or not, and gently sort it the way Sita did: breathe with the part that was in your power, and breathe out the part that never was, letting it rest where it belongs. If you pray, you can place both parts before God. And if a weight ever feels like more than you can carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

1332.title: Draupadi
1332.hook: Krishna's wife visits the forest and asks Draupadi for her secret charm, and Draupadi answers with a list of chores and a treasury
1332.howItsDone: Hindus meet Draupadi in retellings of the Mahabharata, in storytelling and theater, and in some regions as a goddess with her own temples and festivals; her conversation with Satyabhama is read in many ways, from a model of devotion to a portrait of a capable queen.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Sita answered Rama in front of the army, then asked for a fire. Now the other epic.

The question is a little rude, and the guest asks it anyway. The Pandavas are living in the forest, and Krishna comes to visit with his wife Satyabhama. While the men talk, the two women sit together. Satyabhama leans in. Your husbands are heroes, she says, in paraphrase, and they never cross you. How do you do it? Is it a vow? A mantra? Some herb, some charm? Tell me, so Krishna will be like that with me. Draupadi could laugh, or be offended. Instead she gives a long answer, with no magic in it at all. Today: Draupadi, at home.
screen: `A GUEST IN THE FOREST.` → `WHAT'S YOUR SECRET CHARM?` → `AN ANSWER WITH NO MAGIC IN IT.`

segments.voice: Draupadi starts by refusing the premise. Charms and potions, she says in the epic's Forest Book, are a road to ruin. A husband who learns his wife is working spells on him grows afraid of her, the way a person fears a snake in the house. Then she tells Satyabhama what she actually does, and it reads like a day's work. She sets her pride aside. She rises before the household and sleeps after it. She sees that guests are fed and the servants looked after. Then comes a line some readers stop on. Back when they ruled at Indraprastha, she says, the brothers left the burden of the household's income and spending to her. She alone kept track of it. That changes the picture. The woman remembered from the dice hall, dragged in by her hair, was also the one who knew where the kingdom's money went. It's practical, too: Satyabhama wants a shortcut, and Draupadi hands her a routine. And it's honestly debated. Some readers hear a model of devotion in this speech. Others hear a capable woman running a royal house, in the language her world had for it. Others are uneasy with an ideal built so much around serving. The epic gives the speech and lets readers argue. One more thing: Draupadi says all this in exile, with no palace and no treasury left. She describes the work she did there from memory, plainly, without complaint.
screen: `CHARMS ARE A ROAD TO RUIN` · `A DAY'S WORK, NOT A SPELL` · `SHE KEPT THE KINGDOM'S ACCOUNTS` · `READERS HEAR IT DIFFERENT WAYS`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one ordinary day in your home, or a home you grew up in, and ask who kept track of things: the food, the bills, the guests, the small repairs. Let one person come to mind, maybe you, and without judging whether it was fair, let each breath out thank them silently. If you pray, you can name them before God.

1333.title: Draupadi
1333.hook: hungry sages are bathing at the river, the vessel is empty because Draupadi has eaten, and Krishna arrives asking for food
1333.howItsDone: Hindus hear the story of Durvasa's visit in retellings of the Mahabharata and in devotional storytelling, where the vessel of plenty and Krishna eating the last leaf are told as signs of his care for those who call on him.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi at home: asked for a charm, she gave a list of chores and remembered keeping the accounts at Indraprastha.

Dinner is over. The plates are washed. The cook has finally sat down and eaten her own meal. Then there's a knock. A great sage is at the door, with a crowd of disciples behind him, and they would like to be fed. They're going down to the river to bathe first. They'll be back soon. Hungry. In the forest years of the Mahabharata, this is Draupadi's evening, and the sage is Durvasa, remembered for his temper and his curses. Today: an empty pot, and the guest who scraped it.
screen: `THE MEAL IS OVER.` → `A SAGE AT THE DOOR, WITH DISCIPLES.` → `AN EMPTY POT.`

segments.voice: First, the pot. Early in the exile, the epic says, the sun gives Yudhishthira a vessel that will feed the household and its guests every day, until Draupadi has eaten. So Draupadi serves everyone first and eats last, and then the vessel is done for the day. That rule is the whole problem. Some tellings carry the next part. Duryodhana, hoping to trap his cousins, sends Durvasa to visit at exactly the wrong hour, after Draupadi has eaten. The sage and his disciples go off to bathe. Draupadi has nothing to give them, and a sage refused hospitality might curse the house. So she turns to Krishna in her mind, and Krishna arrives. His first words, in paraphrase: I'm hungry. Give me something to eat. Draupadi is almost in despair. The pot is empty, she tells him; that's why I called you. He asks to see it anyway. Stuck to the rim is one small bit of leaf, a scrap of vegetable. Krishna eats it, and says, may this satisfy the one who is the soul of the world. Down at the river, the sages suddenly feel full, as if they'd eaten a feast. Embarrassed to come back and refuse a meal, they slip away. It's funny: the rescuer shows up asking to be fed. It's tender: Krishna takes the scrap no one would serve a guest. And it puts Draupadi at the center of the household. The food lasts until she eats. Everyone's meal is measured by her patience.
screen: `A VESSEL THAT FEEDS UNTIL SHE EATS` · `A SAGE ARRIVES AFTER THE MEAL` · `KRISHNA COMES ASKING FOR FOOD` · `ONE LEAF ON THE RIM`

segments.voice: Bring to mind a time you had almost nothing left to give, no time, no energy, no patience, and just see the empty pot without arguing with it. Then look again, slowly, for one small thing still on the rim, a kind word, five minutes, a glass of water, and let each breath out make that small thing enough for now. If you pray, you can offer it, the way Draupadi turned to Krishna.
Draupadi. She served everyone first, and when the pot was empty and guests were coming, Krishna made a meal of one leaf on the rim. Today's word.
Your line: Draupadi. One leaf on the rim was enough. I'll be here tomorrow.

1334.title: Draupadi
1334.hook: the man who killed her sons in their sleep is dragged before her in ropes, and in the Bhagavata's telling she asks for him to be set free
1334.howItsDone: Hindus who read or hear the Bhagavata Purana meet this scene early in its first book, sometimes in long public recitations, and storytellers set it beside the Mahabharata's own telling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Draupadi and the empty pot: Krishna arrived hungry and made a meal of one leaf on the rim.

Ropes around his arms, Ashvatthama is pushed forward and made to stand in front of her. He is the son of Drona, the Pandavas' own teacher. On the last night of the war he crept into their sleeping camp and killed Draupadi's sons. Arjuna has caught him and tied him up like an animal. Krishna has told Arjuna he may kill him. Instead, Arjuna brings him to the mother of the dead. Last year on this path, the Mahabharata's telling of this moment ended with a jewel. Today the Bhagavata Purana tells it, and she says something else.
screen: `THE KILLER, IN ROPES.` → `BROUGHT TO THE MOTHER.` → `THE BHAGAVATA TELLS IT.`

segments.voice: In the Bhagavata Purana's first book, Draupadi sees the son of her husbands' teacher bound and ashamed, and she bows to him. Then she speaks, in paraphrase. Let him go. Let him go. He is the son of the teacher from whom you learned your bows and your weapons. In him, the teacher is still here. Then the line the whole scene turns on: his mother, Kripi, is still alive. Don't let her weep the way I am weeping now. The text calls her words fair, kind and full of dharma, and some of those present agree. Bhima does not. This man killed sleeping children, he says, and deserves to die. Krishna finds a way through. Arjuna cuts the jewel from Ashvatthama's head and shaves his hair, a punishment the text treats as a kind of death for one like him, and sends him out of the camp alive. Set the two tellings side by side, without ranking them. In the Mahabharata, Draupadi refuses food until she sees the jewel taken from his head. In the Bhagavata, she asks for his life. Readers have held both. Her grief doesn't vanish; she names it, I am weeping. Her mercy doesn't excuse him; the punishment still falls. And the reason she gives is another mother. She doesn't ask what he deserves. She asks who else will be sitting where she is sitting tonight.
screen: `SHE BOWS TO THE BOUND MAN` · `HE IS OUR TEACHER'S SON` · `LET HIS MOTHER NOT WEEP AS I DO` · `TWO TELLINGS, BOTH HELD`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who hurt you, small or large; you don't have to forgive them in this sit, and Draupadi's mercy doesn't erase the harm. Just look past the person, once, to someone who loves them, a mother, a child, a friend, and let that person be there for a few breaths. If you pray, you can hold that other person in prayer. If the hurt is still happening, or grief is too much, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.

1335.title: Kunti
1335.hook: Krishna's chariot is ready to leave, and his aunt Kunti stops him to ask for a strange gift: more trouble
1335.howItsDone: Hindu devotees, especially in Krishna traditions, recite and teach Kunti's prayers from the Bhagavata Purana, and some storytellers at Bhagavata recitations stop to explain her request for hardship.

segments.voice: Three days with Draupadi ended with her sons' killer in ropes, and her asking that his mother not weep as she did.

Call when you get there. Come back soon. Those are goodbye requests. The war is over, the Pandavas are on the throne, and Krishna's chariot is ready to take him home to Dvaraka. His aunt Kunti, the mother of the Pandavas, comes out to see him off. She has lost a husband, hidden in forests, seen her sons gambled into exile and then sent to war. She has finally reached a quiet season. And at the chariot she asks him for something hard to imagine wanting. Today: Kunti, and the gift she wanted.
screen: `A GOODBYE AT THE CHARIOT.` → `A HARD LIFE, A QUIET SEASON.` → `A STRANGE REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The scene sits in the first book of the Bhagavata Purana, and devotees know it as Kunti's prayer. She begins by remembering. You saved us, she tells Krishna, in paraphrase: from poison, from the house of lac, from the forest, from the dice hall, from the weapons of great warriors. Then the request. In Sanskrit it begins vipadah santu tah shashvat: let those troubles come again and again. Why? Because in trouble we saw you, and seeing you is the end of the round of births. She goes further. Wealth, birth, learning and beauty, she says, can make a person too proud to call on God. Those who have nothing are the ones who turn to him. It turns a request inside out: she doesn't ask for ease; she asks for whatever keeps her looking at Krishna. And it's honest about memory. Kunti knows exactly what the hard years cost; she lists them. She isn't romanticizing pain. She's saying what she found inside it. It's a reading, not a rule. Some devotional teachers read this prayer as the heart of surrender. Other readers are wary of wishing hardship on anyone, and say Kunti speaks for herself, not for every sufferer. The text gives it to her as her own prayer, from her own life. And she ends gently, asking Krishna to cut the ties of affection that bind her to her families, so that her mind can flow toward him like a river to the sea.
screen: `SHE REMEMBERS EVERY DANGER` · `LET THOSE TROUBLES COME AGAIN` · `IN TROUBLE, WE SAW YOU` · `HER PRAYER, FROM HER OWN LIFE`

You don't have to wish it back, as Kunti did; just let what you found sit with you for a few breaths. If you pray, you can give thanks for what you were shown.

1336.title: Kunti
1336.hook: in hiding at Ekachakra, Kunti hears her host's family weeping over whose turn it is to die, and offers one of her own sons instead
1336.howItsDone: Hindus meet the Ekachakra story in retellings of the Mahabharata, in children's books and in storytelling, often told as Bhima's adventure, with Kunti's choice at its center.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti at the chariot, asking Krishna for troubles to come again, because in trouble she saw him.

Through a thin wall, in a borrowed room, a mother hears another family crying. Years before the war, after the house of lac burned, Kunti and her sons are hiding in a town called Ekachakra, dressed as poor brahmins, living with a brahmin family who took them in. One evening the house fills with weeping. Kunti goes to find out why. Tomorrow, the family tells her, it's their turn. A demon named Baka lives near the town, and each household in turn must send him a cart of food and a person to be eaten with it. Now they're arguing over who should go. Today: what Kunti says next.
screen: `A BORROWED ROOM IN EKACHAKRA.` → `THE HOST FAMILY WEEPS.` → `IT'S THEIR TURN TOMORROW.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Mahabharata's first book, and it starts with the family. The father says he will go. The mother says no, she will; he can find another wife, but the children need a father. The daughter says send me; I'm the one you'll lose to marriage anyway. And the small son picks up a blade of grass, waves it, and says he'll kill the demon with that. Then Kunti speaks, in paraphrase. You have sheltered us; let me repay you. I have five sons, and one of them will take the food to Baka. The brahmin refuses. He can't let a guest die for him. Kunti insists, and tells him the son she has in mind is strong. When the brothers come home, Yudhishthira is upset: you're risking our brother on a stranger's trouble? Kunti's answer is calm. She has thought it through. She has seen Bhima's strength since he was a baby. And repaying the people who sheltered them is dharma; the town, too, will be better for it. So Bhima goes, eats the demon's food in front of him to make him angry, and kills him. It's a portrait of a mother who doesn't panic: she weighs it, and decides. It's about debt: a guest, to her, owes something to the house. And it shows a woman steering the family. Her eldest son questions her. The decision is hers.

If something feels unrepaid, you don't have to fix it now; Kunti weighed things before she acted, and you can simply hold that person with each breath. If you pray, you can give thanks for them.

1337.hook: before the war, Kunti gives Krishna a message for her sons, and the message is a story about another mother who would not let her son lie down

segments.voice: Yesterday, Kunti at Ekachakra, offering one of her own sons to repay the family who sheltered them.

Krishna's peace mission has failed. Before he leaves Hastinapura, he goes to see his aunt, who has stayed behind in the city while her sons waited out their exile. He asks if she has a message for them. She does, but she doesn't start with advice. She starts with a story, an old one, she says, about a woman named Vidula and her son. Kunti wants her sons to hear it before the war. Today, at the end of a week of the epics' women, Kunti speaks through someone else's voice.
screen: `THE PEACE MISSION HAS FAILED.` → `A MESSAGE FOR HER SONS.` → `SHE TELLS THEM A STORY.`

segments.voice: The story is in the Mahabharata's Book of Effort, here in paraphrase. Vidula is a proud woman of a warrior family. Her son Sanjaya has been beaten by a rival king, and now he lies at home, low and listless. Vidula goes to him, and she is not gentle. Get up, she tells him. You were not born to lie here. Then this line, which in Sanskrit runs muhurtam jvalitam shreyo, na tu dhumayitam ciram: better to blaze up for a moment than to smolder for a long time. Her son argues back. What good will a kingdom be to you, he asks, if I'm dead? She answers him again and again until he rises. Then Kunti adds her own words to Krishna, for Arjuna and Bhima: the time has come for which a mother of warriors bears sons. Kunti, who asked Krishna for trouble in the Bhagavata, here asks her sons to walk toward it. She doesn't only command; she tells a story and lets it work. It's not a comfortable passage. Some readers hear courage; others hear the cost of a war a mother has just urged. The epic keeps both. And it closes a week of women: Sita, answering Rama before the army; Draupadi, keeping accounts, waiting by an empty pot, asking for a killer's life; and Kunti, who sends a story ahead of her sons.
screen: `VIDULA AND HER BEATEN SON` · `BLAZE A MOMENT, DON'T SMOLDER` · `KUNTI SPEAKS THROUGH THE STORY` · `A WEEK OF THE EPICS' WOMEN`

segments.voice: Ask gently whether one thing in your life has been smoldering a long time, a call or a task you keep not starting, and don't scold yourself: Vidula's words were for a warrior, and yours can be kinder. Let it come into view, warmth gathering around it like an ember on each breath in, one first step appearing on each breath out. If you pray, you can ask for courage. And if low days ever start to feel like there's no point, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
